557	\label{app:shapley}

559	We quantify each method's marginal contribution to the MMCT ensemble using Shapley values~\cite{shapley1953value}, computed via exact enumeration over all $2^5{=}32$ coalitions of the five detection methods.
560	For a coalition $S \subseteq \{m_1, \ldots, m_5\}$, we define two performance metrics: the false positive rate FPR($S$), computed from 3 null experiments ($\alpha{=}0.0$, seeds 42/43/44; 24 null pairs total), and the false negative rate FNR($S$), computed from 45 signal experiments across all non-null $\alpha$ levels (270 signal pairs for the 6-pair variant excluding mauve).
561	The Shapley value $\phi_k$ for method $m_k$ is the weighted average of its marginal contribution across all coalitions; positive FPR-Shapley indicates the method \emph{increases} false positives, while negative FNR-Shapley indicates it \emph{reduces} false negatives.
562	The combined Shapley value $\phi_k^{\text{comb}} = \phi_k^{\text{FPR}} + \phi_k^{\text{FNR}}$ balances both error types, with more negative values indicating greater net benefit.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}

\paragraph{Methodological pitfalls.}
\label{sec:pitfalls}
Lead-lag analysis in iterative model collapse is fragile along three axes, each documented with data from \S\ref{sec:regime}--\ref{sec:dose_response}.
\emph{Method sensitivity}: five detection methods applied to identical data ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs, direction-checked) yield forward significance rates spanning 0\% to 75\%, with inter-method agreement at $\kappa{=}0.185$ and naive cross-correlation reaching 75\% null-control FPR.
\emph{Spurious regression}: first-differencing to remove shared trends~\cite{granger1974spurious} eliminates canary$\to$perplexity associations ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$) while preserving canary$\to$diversity (24/24$\to$24/24), exposing an entire analysis channel as trend-driven rather than temporally precedent.
\emph{Regime dependence}: the same Granger test finds 0/8 pairs significant through $\alpha{=}0.45$ but 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, a categorical shift at a 5-percentage-point boundary that a single-$\alpha$ study would miss entirely.
These pitfalls motivate systematic method comparison rather than reliance on any single detection approach.

\paragraph{Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT).}
\label{sec:mmct}
We apply the Multi-Method Consensus Test, a weighted consensus framework in the specification curve~\cite{simonsohn2020specification} and multi-method early-warning~\cite{scheffer2009early,bell2022modeling} traditions, adapted to the constraints of iterative training analysis: short series ($T{=}5$--$20$), non-stationarity by design, and heterogeneous method sensitivities.
MMCT is a consensus testing protocol, not a novel statistical method.
It compares five lead-lag detection methods through FPR-inverse weighted consensus, calibrated against null-control ($\alpha{=}0.0$) data where any detection is a false positive.
Each method $m_k$ receives weight $w_k = 1/\max(\hat{\text{FPR}}_k, \epsilon)$ with $\epsilon{=}0.01$; the weighted score $W(X \to Y) = \sum_k w_k d_k / \sum_k w_k$ yields formal $p$-values from the empirical null distribution (Appendix).
MMCT identifies permutation Granger (PermG) as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with consistent detection across contamination levels, and we recommend it as the primary detection method based on this systematic comparison.

\paragraph{Permutation Granger causality.}
PermG tests whether past values of canary metric $X$ improve prediction of downstream metric $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history; Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causality~\cite{shojaie2022granger}.
We apply 5{,}000 permutations~\citep{phipson2010permutation} on first-differenced series with Benjamini--Hochberg FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$ across 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (2 canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics).
Three properties distinguish PermG: a nonparametric null distribution robust to the short non-stationary series typical of iterative training~\cite{boettiger2012limits}, built-in directionality (forward and reverse tested separately), and a hyperparameter-free test statistic.
The remaining four methods each exhibit a specific limitation: naive cross-correlation has 75\% null-control FPR; differenced cross-correlation detects bidirectionally without directional separation; threshold onset is power-limited at $T{=}11$ under corrected $3\sigma$ calibration (0/8 significant in 8 of 12 cross-architecture conditions); Toda--Yamamoto~\cite{toda1995statistical} achieves moderate supplementary detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) with reduced power from degree-of-freedom costs of lag augmentation.
Per-method dose-response profiles, Shapley value analysis, and the full MMCT algorithm appear in the Appendix.

\subsection{Signal-Times-Resolution Interpretive Lens}
\label{sec:theory}

We apply standard statistical power scaling to PermG, interpreted through a Signal$\times$Resolution (S$\times$R) decomposition.
Detectability of canary$\to$downstream temporal precedence depends on two competing factors:
\begin{equation}
    \text{Detectability}(\alpha) \;\propto\; S(\alpha) \times R(\alpha),
    \label{eq:detectability}
\end{equation}
where $S(\alpha)$ is signal strength (magnitude of distributional shift, monotonically increasing with $\alpha$) and $R(\alpha)$ is temporal resolution (the generational gap between canary and downstream responses).
$R(\alpha)$ is non-monotonic: at low $\alpha$, entropy and diversity respond in different generations ($R$ large); at $\alpha{\approx}0.60$, relaxation time matching compresses both responses into a single generation ($R \to 0$); at high $\alpha$, the severity of entropy collapse outpaces the diversity cascade, restoring the generational offset.
The product $S \times R$ predicts four regimes: \emph{blind} ($\alpha \leq 0.45$; $S$ below detection floor), \emph{onset} ($\alpha \approx 0.50$; $S$ crosses threshold while $R$ remains high), \emph{synchronous dip} ($\alpha \approx 0.60$; $R \to 0$ suppresses detection despite rising $S$), and \emph{detection} ($\alpha \geq 0.75$; $S$ dominates).
Full empirical confirmation appears in \S\ref{sec:regime} and \S\ref{sec:dose_response}.

Under a permutation test framework, detection power scales as $\mathrm{Power}(\alpha, T) = \Phi\bigl(S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T} / \sigma_{\mathrm{noise}}\bigr)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF and the $\sqrt{T}$ scaling follows standard power analysis as a conservative lower bound.
This instantiates the standard $z$-test power formula; the contribution is the empirical decomposition into signal $S(\alpha)$ and resolution $R(\alpha)$ components and the identification of $R(\alpha)$ non-monotonicity.
The sharp detection onset at $\alpha_c$ (at $T{=}10$) is consistent with a power threshold: when $S \cdot R \cdot \sqrt{T}$ first exceeds the detection floor, power undergoes a steep onset from near-zero to near-one.
This generates three predictions for $T{=}20$: (i)~$\alpha_c$ left-shifts as increased $T$ raises power at all $\alpha$; (ii)~the transition smooths as $\sqrt{T}$ broadens the power curve; (iii)~different methods exhibit different $\alpha_c$ values due to method-specific power curves.
Bootstrap calibration ($N{=}10{,}000$) yields clean falsifiable tests at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$: predicted 7/8 (95\% CI: [6,8]); results below 6/8 would falsify $\sqrt{T}$ power scaling.
At $\alpha{=}0.45$, the point prediction is 0/8, but the bootstrap CI spans [0,7] reflecting $\alpha_c$ uncertainty---both detection and non-detection are informative for constraining the phase boundary location.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$, the prediction is inherently uncertain at the transition (CI: [0,7]).
Sub-threshold FDR $p{=}0.059$--$0.091$ at $\alpha{=}0.45$ is consistent with proximity to the power boundary.

\subsection{Canary-Based Early Intervention: Proof of Concept}
\label{sec:intervention}

We implement a predictive cessation protocol: training with synthetic data ($\alpha{=}1.0$) continues until token entropy drops ${>}15\%$ relative to generation~0, at which point $\alpha$ switches to $0.0$ (pure real data).
A reactive baseline triggers when distinct-1 drops ${>}10\%$.
The predictive trigger fires at generation~1 in both Pythia-410M and Pythia-1.4B (s42 fp32), one generation before the reactive baseline (generation~2).
Peak perplexity under predictive intervention is $56.99$ versus $157.09$ under reactive (s42 fp32), a 58\% reduction (bootstrap 95\% CI: 29--64\%).
Recovery occurs at generation~2 under predictive cessation versus generation~4 under reactive.
Both models converge to the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline by generation~10.

The trigger generation, recovery timeline, and convergence behavior are identical across the $3.4\times$ scale gap from 410M to 1.4B.
This proof-of-concept illustrates the potential for canary-based intervention; the 15\% threshold was selected post hoc, and threshold sensitivity analysis is left to future work.
The four-layer detection taxonomy and practical guidance tiers appear in Appendix~\ref{app:extended_discussion}.

\section{Channel Effect Size Analysis}
\label{app:channel_effect_size}

First-differencing eliminates all canary$\to$perplexity Granger associations while preserving canary$\to$diversity leads (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
We present three lines of evidence that this asymmetry reflects a genuine temporal structure difference rather than selective power loss from differencing.

\paragraph{Correlation retention parity.}
First-differencing retains comparable correlation magnitude for both channel types (Table~\ref{tab:channel_retention}).
Diversity channels ($n{=}243$ pairs across all non-null experiments) retain a median $|r|$ of 0.952 after differencing, while perplexity channels ($n{=}8$ pairs; limited sample) retain 1.00.
This parity rules out a blanket power-loss explanation: if differencing selectively destroyed perplexity signal, $|r|$ retention would be substantially lower for perplexity than for diversity.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{First-differencing effect by channel type. $|r|$ retention = diff $|r|$ / naive $|r|$. Despite comparable $|r|$ retention, Granger $F$ differs by an order of magnitude. Perplexity channel has limited sample ($n{=}8$); all paired comparisons are from bf16 experiments.}
\label{tab:channel_retention}
\begin{tabular}{lrccrc}
\toprule
Channel & $n$ & Naive $|r|$ & Diff $|r|$ & Retention & Med.\ $F$ \\
\midrule
Diversity   & 243 & 0.943 & 0.921 & 0.952 & 67.8 \\
Perplexity  & 8   & 0.924 & 0.900 & 1.002 & 11.5 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Granger $F$-statistic asymmetry.}
Within matched experiments (same model, seed, $\alpha$, precision), the Granger $F$-statistic is $20$--$28{\times}$ higher for diversity than perplexity channels.
At $\alpha{=}0.60$ (s42, bf16): diversity mean $F{=}229.4$ versus perplexity mean $F{=}8.3$ (ratio $27.8{\times}$).
At $\alpha{=}1.0$ reactive (s43, bf16): diversity mean $F{=}236.4$ versus perplexity mean $F{=}11.5$ (ratio $20.6{\times}$).
Since $|r|$ retention is comparable across channels, this $F$-statistic gap cannot be attributed to differencing-induced signal loss; it must reflect a difference in the temporal structure that Granger tests evaluate.

\paragraph{Temporal structure: lagged vs.\ contemporaneous.}
The lag distribution of peak differenced cross-correlations reveals the structural difference.
For diversity channels, 81\% of peak correlations occur at canary-leading lags (lag${<}0$), with a median lag of $-1$ generation---consistent with the one-generation temporal precedence visible in Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory}.
For perplexity channels, 50\% of peak correlations occur at lag${=}0$ (contemporaneous co-movement), with a median lag of $0$.
Granger causality tests lagged predictive improvement; contemporaneous co-movement produces low $F$-statistics regardless of signal magnitude, which is the correct behavior for a test designed to detect temporal precedence.
The perplexity channel sample is limited ($n{=}8$ pairs from bf16 experiments), and these lag distributions should not be generalized to fp32 conditions without further validation.
